clinicalPearls: A malignancy that arises almost exclusively in the minor salivary glands, with the palate being the classic site of origin.
It is one of the commonest intraoral minor salivary gland malignancies and typically presents as a painless, slow-growing submucosal swelling.
The defining paradox is cytological uniformity combined with architectural diversity: tubular, cribriform, solid, single-file streaming and concentric targetoid patterns coexist.
Perineural invasion, often with a targetoid whorling pattern, is common yet usually consistent with indolent behaviour.
The classic type harbours a recurrent PRKD1 hotspot mutation, whereas the cribriform-predominant variant more often shows PRKD1, PRKD2 or PRKD3 rearrangements.
Tumour cells are typically S100 positive with a low proliferation index, and the main task is to separate it from adenoid cystic carcinoma.
The cribriform variant, favouring the tongue base, more frequently involves regional lymph nodes yet still generally behaves indolently.
Wide local excision is the mainstay, and distinguishing it from adenoid cystic carcinoma has major implications for treatment intensity.
reference.pathophysiology: Polymorphous adenocarcinoma is a malignant neoplasm derived from the terminal duct or intercalated duct cells of minor salivary glands, in which a single, cytologically bland cell population expresses a remarkably wide range of growth patterns. In most conventional tumours an activating hotspot mutation in the PRKD1 gene deregulates protein kinase D signalling, driving proliferation, while the cribriform-predominant variant is instead characterised by rearrangements of PRKD1, PRKD2 or PRKD3. The neoplastic cells infiltrate the surrounding tissue in tubules, cribriform islands, solid nests and single-file cords, and characteristically ensheath nerves in concentric layers, so that perineural invasion is a defining rather than an alarming feature. Despite this infiltrative and neurotropic growth, proliferative activity remains low, which underlies the tumour's generally indolent clinical course.
additionalInvestigations: Incisional biopsy of the mucosal or submucosal lesion
Immunohistochemistry including S100 and Ki-67 proliferation index
MRI to assess soft-tissue extent and perineural spread
Molecular testing for PRKD1 alterations where available
CT to evaluate bony involvement of the palate or maxilla
Ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging of the neck for nodal assessment
redFlags: Bone invasion of the palate or maxilla
Regional nodal metastasis, particularly with the cribriform variant
Solid, high-grade-appearing areas within the tumour
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable and the tumour is low-grade, with complete excision usually curative. The cribriform variant carries a higher rate of nodal metastasis but still tends to behave indolently, whereas misdiagnosis as adenoid cystic carcinoma risks unnecessary overtreatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as adenoid cystic carcinoma, leading to inappropriate treatment intensity
Achieving inadequate margins because of the infiltrative growth pattern
Failing to recognise the characteristic perineural invasion
Mistaking it for a benign pleomorphic adenoma on a small biopsy

management: Complete surgical excision with clear margins as the curative mainstay for this low-grade minor salivary gland malignancy
Neck dissection where nodal metastasis is present, particularly in the cribriform-predominant variant
Adjuvant radiotherapy reserved for positive or close margins, extensive perineural invasion or recurrent disease
Accurate histopathological distinction from adenoid cystic carcinoma, aided by S100 positivity and a low Ki-67 index, to avoid unnecessary overtreatment
Long-term clinical and imaging surveillance for local recurrence and late nodal or distant metastasis
Head and neck multidisciplinary team management of surgery, pathology, reconstruction and rehabilitation
